core_principles.text: The standard push-up requires a general stiffening of the knee joints, hip joints, pelvis, and spine to keep the body in a straight line from head to feet.
During the push-up, the shoulders and elbows must flex and extend to raise and lower the body while the scapulae retract and protract to facilitate glenohumeral range of motion.

common_mistakes.text: Placing the hands in a very narrow position tends to encourage flaring of the elbows, orienting movement into the transverse plane.

specific_findings.text: The knee push-up shortens the lever, reducing bodyweight loading to 54% in the top position and 62% in the bottom position.
The standard push-up requires supporting 69% of bodyweight in the top position and 75% of bodyweight in the bottom position.
Compressive spinal loading on the L4/L5 joint reaches 1,838 N during a standard push-up.
Mean muscle activation normalized to maximum voluntary contraction during a standard push-up is 61% for the pectoralis major, 66% for the triceps brachii, and 42% for the anterior deltoid.
Narrow base push-ups (50% shoulder width) elicit greater activation of the triceps brachii and promote superior activation of the sternal head of the pectoralis major compared to a wide base.

core_principles.text: Shifting the torso forward relative to the hands results in increased pectoralis major activity and decreased triceps brachii activity compared with the normal base position.
Shifting the torso rearward relative to the hands results in slightly increased pectoralis major and triceps brachii activity.

Performing push-ups with the hands on an unstable surface like a stability ball increases the activation of the triceps brachii, pectoralis major, rectus abdominis, and external obliques compared with push-ups on a bench from the same angle.
Unstable surfaces are more effective at increasing muscle activity when they serve as the primary base of support under the hands rather than under the feet.
Suspended push-ups activate more core musculature than standard push-ups.

specific_findings.text: Ebben et al. found that push-ups with the hands elevated on a 61.0-cm box require supporting 41% of bodyweight.
Ebben et al. found that knee push-ups require supporting 49% of bodyweight.
Ebben et al. found that push-ups with the hands elevated on a 30.5-cm box require supporting 55% of bodyweight.
Ebben et al. found that regular push-ups require supporting 64% of bodyweight.
Ebben et al. found that push-ups with the feet elevated on a 30.5-cm box require supporting 70% of bodyweight.
Ebben et al. found that push-ups with the feet elevated on a 61.0-cm box require supporting 74% of bodyweight.
BOSU push-ups increase the activity of the upper, mid, and lower trapezius fibers, but diminish serratus anterior activity compared with standard push-ups.
Lehman et al. reported that elevating the feet above the hands had a greater stimulus on scapulothoracic stabilizing musculature than placing the hands on a stability ball.

Youdas et al. found no significant differences in EMG activity of the triceps brachii, pectoralis major, serratus anterior, and posterior deltoids when comparing the Perfect Push-up to standard push-ups.

core_principles.text: The countermovement push-up, characterized by fast eccentric, reversal, and concentric phases without leaving the ground, is a safe and effective choice for explosive variations to maximize upper-body power without encountering impact forces.
Wall push-ups and knee push-ups are appropriate regressions to decrease the challenge for individuals with limited upper-body strength.
Push-ups using one arm or one leg, weighted vests, elastic bands, chains, or unstable implements can be used to increase the difficulty of the exercise.
Practitioners should select push-up variations that optimize the challenge on the target musculature without compromising proper form and risking injury.

common_mistakes.text: Performing advanced forms of plyometric push-ups, such as alternating plyometric push-ups using a medicine ball, when having pre-existing back issues.

specific_findings.text: Clapping push-ups outperform standard, slow eccentric, 1 hand on medicine ball, staggered hands, hands on 2 balls, 2 hands on 1 ball, rapid countermovement, 1 arm, and alternating plyometric push-up variations in pectoralis major and triceps brachii activity.
An alternating plyometric push-up using a medicine ball has been shown to induce 6,224 N of compressive forces on the lumbar spine.
The countermovement push-up, performed with maximal speed, exhibits the highest peak force and rate of force development among explosive variations.

consequences.text: Performing advanced plyometric push-ups like the alternating medicine ball variation can be problematic for individuals with back issues because it induces 6,224 N of compressive forces on the lumbar spine.
